agency_premium_multiplier.citation: NSI Nursing Solutions, 2026 NSI National Health Care Retention & RN Staffing Report: hospital average travel nurse fee $91.23/hour against hospital average RN pay $59.46/hour including 25.8% for benefits (so $47.27 base wage); 'nurse travel rates average $91/hour and range to $160/hour'. Value = 91.23 / 47.27.
agency_premium_multiplier.note: DERIVED ratio of the travel-nurse bill rate to base RN wage (the unit of this attribute is x wage, before benefits). Against the benefits-loaded staff cost the premium is 1.53x. High end = $160/hour. Industry survey of 527 US hospitals, calendar 2025; registered nurses only.

benefits_load.citation: NSI Nursing Solutions, 2026 NSI National Health Care Retention & RN Staffing Report: 'Hospital Average RN Pay (includes 25.8% for benefits) $59.46' per hour.
benefits_load.note: Registered nurses, industry survey, US 2025. High end of the range is a judgement, not from the source. Replace with BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation if the data workstream extracts it.

shift_hours.citation: Placeholder set in Wave 0 so the simulator can run; three 8-hour shifts 07-15, 15-23, 23-07 (many EDs run 12s; simplified)

absence_rate.citation: BLS Current Population Survey, annual averages 2025, Table 47: Absences from work of employed full-time wage and salary workers by occupation and industry: lost worktime rate, total, for 'Healthcare practitioners and technical occupations' = 2.1 percent of usual hours
absence_rate.note: Published table value, transcribed (bls.gov blocks scripted download; read via a fetch tool twice with matching figures - re-verify in a browser). Lost worktime rate = hours absent / hours usually worked, the closest published analogue of a share of scheduled shifts missed. range upper end = the absence rate of healthcare support occupations (4.1% of workers absent in the reference week; practitioners 3.7%). 2025 averages exclude October. Wave 0 placeholder was 0.035.

fatigue_error_multiplier.citation: Landrigan CP et al. (2004) Effect of reducing interns' work hours on serious medical errors in intensive care units, N Engl J Med 351:1838-48 (randomised; 2,203 patient-days): 35.9% more serious medical errors on the traditional schedule with 24 h+ shifts (136.0 vs 100.1 per 1,000 patient-days), 5.6 times as many serious diagnostic errors. Barger LK et al. (2006) PLoS Med 3(12):e487 (2,737 interns, 17,003 monthly reports, self-report): odds ratio 3.5 (3.3-3.7) of a fatigue-related significant medical error in months with 1-4 extended shifts and 7.5 with 5 or more.
fatigue_error_multiplier.note: Value set inside a loose range: 1.36 is the observed-error ratio from the trial, 3.5 the self-reported odds ratio. Both are interns on 24 h+ shifts, US, 2002-2005; no direct estimate exists for 8-12 h ED shifts. Nurses: Rogers AE et al. (2004) Health Aff 23(4):202-12 found error risk significantly higher past 12 h, with overtime and past 40 h/week (393 nurses, 5,317 shifts; effect size not in the abstract). Second URL: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0030487

annual_turnover.citation: NSI Nursing Solutions, 2026 NSI National Health Care Retention & RN Staffing Report (survey of 527 hospitals in 40 states, calendar year 2025): hospital turnover 18.5% (range 7.6% to 33.1%); RN turnover 17.6%; RN turnover by specialty chart, Emergency about 20.7% in 2025 and 19.1% in 2024; average cost of turnover for one bedside RN $60,090; each 1% change in RN turnover about $295,000/year for the average hospital.
annual_turnover.note: Value is the all-staff hospital rate because this attribute is shared by every role; use about 0.21 for ED nurses. Industry survey (self-selected respondents), US, 2025. The emergency-specialty figures were read from a chart whose year legend was inferred from the text of the report.

rn_patients_per_nurse_max.citation: California Code of Regulations, Title 22, section 70217(a)(8): 'The licensed nurse-to-patient ratio in an emergency department shall be 1:4 or fewer at all times'; 1:2 or fewer for critical care patients in the ED; minimum 1:1 registered nurse for critical trauma patients; at least two licensed nurses present when a patient is present, one RN assigned to triage. Other units in the same section: critical care 1:2, step-down 1:3, telemetry 1:4, medical/surgical 1:5.
rn_patients_per_nurse_max.note: Regulation, not a measurement. California is the enforced precedent. New Jersey: no ED ratio of this kind is in force; Assembly bill A1974 ('Patient Protection and Safe Staffing Act', pre-filed for introduction in the 2026 session, https://pub.njleg.state.nj.us/Bills/2026/A2000/1974_I1.PDF) would require 1 RN : 4 ED patients, 1:2 ED critical care, 1:1 ED trauma; it is a bill, not law. Range low end 1 = trauma, 2 = critical care.
